Infections 169 Penicillins The penicillins are bactericidal antibacterial drugs that interfere with bacterial cell -wall synthesis. The various penicillins share a common structure and mechanism of action; their distribution in the body is extensive but penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid is poor except when the meninges are inflamed. They are mainly excreted in the urine. These drugs are remarkably free of toxic effects, but in renal failure large doses may cause convulsions and coma. The most serious adverse effect is hypersensitivity, which may result in anaphylactic shock and is occasionally fatal. Cross -sensitivity occurs with all penicillins and with other beta -lactam compounds (cephalospor ins, carbapenems). interactions: Immunomodulatory agents (lenalidomide, thalidomide, pomalidomide): Concomitant use with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) may increase the risk of thrombotic and thromboembolic events, particularly in patients with multiple myeloma. Monitor closely for signs and symptoms of thrombosis. Agents associated with thromboembolic risk (estrogens, hormonal contraceptives, and other prothrombotic agents): Co-administration may produce an additive increase in thromboembolic risk. Use with caution and monitor accordingly. Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus): Changes in hematocrit resulting from ESA therapy may alter the blood concentrations of these agents. Monitor calcineurin inhibitor levels and adjust the dose as clinically indicated. Iron and hematinic status: Adequate iron stores are required for an optimal erythropoietic response. Functional or absolute iron deficiency reduces the effectiveness of darbepoetin alfa. Supplemental iron should be administered to maintain transferrin saturation ≥20% and serum ferritin ≥100 mcg/L. General: No dosage adjustment of concomitant medications is required. The principal interaction -related concern is an additive increase in thromboembolic risk when darbepoetin alfa is combi ned with other agents that promote thrombosis. These risks should be considered together with the boxed -warning cautions regarding mortality, cardiovascular events, and tumor progression.

Endocrine System Diabetes mellitus There are two principal types of diabetes. Type 1 (insulin-dependent) is characterised by subnormal or absent insulin secretion and requires daily insulin. Type 2 (non -insulin-dependent) results from reduced insulin secretion or peripheral insulin resistance; many patients are obese and may respond to die t and weight reduction, while others require oral or injectable antidiabetic drugs. Treatment aims to relieve symptoms and minimise long -term microvascular and cardiovascular complications. MUSCULOSKELETAL AND JOINT DISEASES Drugs Used in Rheumatic Diseases and Gout Non-steroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) All NSAIDs are antipyretic, analgesic and anti-inflammatory, with important differences in their activities. As analgesics they are effective only against pain of low to moderate intensity. Chronic post-operative pain and pain arising from inflammation are particularly well controlled by NSAIDs, whereas pain arising from hollow viscera is not relieved. As antipyretics, NSAIDs reduce body temperature in febrile states; however, some are not suitable for routine or prolonged use. The main clinical application is as anti-inflammatory agents in musculoskeletal disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. The main differences between NSAIDs are in the incidence and type of side-effects, so efficacy should always be weighed against possible adverse effects. NSAIDs vary in their selectivity for cyclo-oxygenase (COX) enzymes; non-selective inhibition is thought to underlie the high incidence of GI adverse effects, while selective COX-2 inhibitors are claimed to be relatively free from GI side-effects. warnings: Cautions and warnings: Renal impairment; monitor for signs of hypermagnesaemia (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, heart block). | Adverse drug reactions: Hypotension and asystole with rapid administration. Level >3 mg/dL: CNS depression, diarrhoea, blocked neuromuscular transmission; >5 mg/dL: flushing, somnolence; >12.5 mg/dL: complete heart block, cardiac arrest. | Monitoring: Serum magnesium, deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, blood pressure and ECG; renal function. | Pregnancy category: Magnesium crosses the placenta; serum concentrations in the fetus are similar to those in the mother (Idama 1998; Osada 2002). Continuous maternal use for >5 to 7 days (in doses such as those used for preterm labor, an off-label use) may cause fetal hypocalcemia and bone abnormalities, as well as fractures in the neonate. Magnesium sulfate injection is used for the prevention and treatment of seizures in pregnant or postpartum women with severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia (ACOG 2013; ACOG 652 2016). Magnesium sulfate may also be used prior to early preterm delivery for neuroprotection to reduce the risk of cerebral palsy (ACOG 455 2010; ACOG 652 2016; Reeves 2011); specific regimens are not available, but treatment may be of benefit when birth is anticipated before 32 weeks gestation (ACOG 171 2016; ACOG 172 2016; ACOG 652 2016). Tocolytics 377 may be used for the short-term (48 hour) prolongation of pregnancy to allow for the administration of antenatal steroids and should not be used prior to fetal viability or when the risks of use to the fetus or mother are greater than the risk of preterm birth; maintenance therapy with tocolytics is ineffective and not recommended. Magnesium sulfate can be used up to 48 hours in women at risk of delivery within 7 days; however, it is not the preferred tocolytic (ACOG 171 2016; ACOG 652 2016). | Lactation: Magnesium is found in breast milk; concentrations remain constant during the first year of lactation and are not influenced by dietary intake under normal conditions.
